aiOverview.content: Traveling internationally often requires specific vaccines to protect against diseases not common in the United States, such as yellow fever, typhoid, and Japanese encephalitis. The CDC recommends consulting a healthcare provider or travel clinic 4–6 weeks before departure to allow time for vaccines to take effect and for multi-dose series to be completed. Top Recommended & Required Travel Vaccines Routine Vaccines: Ensure you are up to date on measles-mumps-rubella (MMR), diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, varicella (chickenpox), polio, and your yearly flu shot. Hepatitis A: Recommended for travelers to most countries, particularly those with uncertain water or food safety. Typhoid: Recommended for travelers going to parts of Asia, Africa, and South America, especially if visiting smaller cities, villages, or rural areas. Yellow Fever (Required/Recommended): Required for entry into certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa and South America. Proof of vaccination (the "Yellow Card") is required, which becomes valid 10 days after administration. Meningococcal (Required/Recommended): Required for travelers to Saudi Arabia for Hajj or Umrah pilgrimages, and recommended for the "meningitis belt" of Africa. Other Potential Vaccines: Based on specific itinerary and activities: Rabies, Japanese encephalitis, Tick-borne encephalitis, and COVID-19. Last-Minute Travelers Even if traveling soon, a visit to a travel clinic is still valuable. Some vaccines can be given on an accelerated schedule, and malaria prevention medication can be prescribed. Key Steps Before You Go Check CDC Destination Pages: Visit the CDC Travelers' Health website to find specific recommendations for your destination. CDC Travelers' Health website Find a Clinic: Many travel vaccines are not available at standard pharmacies. Look for a dedicated travel medicine clinic or authorized yellow fever vaccination center. Bring Vaccination Records: Carry a copy of your official immunization records with you. Check Insurance: Travel vaccines are often not covered by standard insurance and can be costly. Disclaimer: Vaccine recommendations can change based on current outbreaks. As of March 2026, the CDC has issued alerts for increased polio risk in over 30 countries.
